prompt: `a := errors.New("not found")` and `b := errors.New("not found")`. What does `a == b` give?

choices.text: `true`, because the messages are equal
choices.why: `a.Error() == b.Error()` was `true`; `a == b` compares the values, and they differ.

choices.text: `false`
choices.why: Right. Each call returns a pointer to a new `errorString`, and the two pointers differ.

choices.text: It does not compile: errors cannot be compared with `==`
choices.why: Interfaces compare with `==`; `a == c` compiled and gave `true`.

choices.text: `true` the first time and `false` after the program has run a while
choices.why: Nothing about it depends on time; two calls give two distinct values from the start.

prompt: After `c := a`, `a == c` is `true`. Why?

choices.text: Because `c` is a reference to the variable `a`
choices.why: Assignment copies a value; `c` is a variable of its own holding a copy of the interface.

choices.text: Because `==` on errors compares their messages
choices.why: Then `a == b` would be `true` as well, and it was `false`.

choices.text: Copying the interface copied its pointer too
choices.why: Right. Same type, same pointer, so both point at one `errorString`: the same error.

choices.text: Because `errors.New` caches the last error it made
choices.why: `New` is one line, `return &errorString{text}`; it keeps nothing between calls.

prompt: Why is `if err.Error() == "not found"` a poor way to recognise a failure?

choices.text: It does not compile, because `Error` returns a pointer
choices.why: `Error` returns a `string`, and comparing strings compiles; that is what makes the test dangerous.

choices.text: Rewording the message breaks it silently
choices.why: Right. And unrelated errors may share the text. The sentence is for a person; the identity is the value.

choices.text: Calling `Error` changes the error
choices.why: `Error` only returns `e.s`; it changes nothing.

choices.text: It is always false, because `Error` adds the type's name to the text
choices.why: `Error` returns the text as given: `fmt.Println(a)` printed `not found` and nothing more.

prompt: `fmt.Printf("%T\n", errors.New("x"))` prints `*errors.___`.
Which message needs `fmt.Errorf` rather than `errors.New`?

choices.text: `name is empty`
choices.why: A fixed sentence with nothing to format is exactly what `errors.New` is for.

choices.text: `age cannot be negative`
choices.why: Lesson 32's `price` built this one with `errors.New`; it never changes.

choices.text: `age -4 is negative`
choices.why: Right. The -4 is the age that was given, and formatting it in takes `%d` and so `fmt.Errorf`.

choices.text: `operation not allowed`
choices.why: Fixed text again; every occurrence says the same thing.

prompt: `fmt.Errorf("read config: %v", err)` and `fmt.Errorf("read config: %w", err)` print the same text. What differs?

choices.text: Only the `%w` one keeps the original error inside it
choices.why: Right. `%w` gave a `*fmt.wrapError` with the error in its `err` field; `%v` gave text only.

choices.text: Only the `%w` one can be printed with `fmt.Println`
choices.why: Both printed: they are the first two lines of the output.

choices.text: The `%v` one is not an `error`, only a string
choices.why: It is an `error`, a `*errors.errorString`; `fmt.Errorf` always returns an error.

choices.text: The `%w` one hides the original message from the output
choices.why: The original message is printed in both; the difference is in what is kept.

prompt: `readConfig` returns `fmt.Errorf("read config: %w", err)` without repeating the file name. Why is leaving it out right?
hint: What does the error from `os.ReadFile` already say?

choices.text: File names are not allowed in error messages
choices.why: Nothing forbids them; the `*fs.PathError` prints one itself.

choices.text: `%w` cannot be combined with a second verb in one format
choices.why: `fmt.Errorf("read %s: %w", path, err)` is allowed; the reason is that it would say the path twice.

choices.text: The caller adds the name later
choices.why: `start` added `start server`, its own step, not the file name.

choices.text: The `*fs.PathError` underneath already names it
choices.why: Right. Each layer adds what the error does not know yet, and the path is already there.

prompt: In `~/wrap-context`, put the parts of the final message in the order the program WROTE them.
items: `open settings.json: no such file or directory`

prompt: `~/wrap-style` printed `Failed to start server: Error: could not read config: open settings.json: no such file or directory..`. Which convention would have prevented the two full stops?

choices.text: Using `%v` instead of `%w`
choices.why: Both verbs print the same text; the full stops were written in the format strings.

choices.text: Starting each message with a capital letter
choices.why: That is the other half of the problem, `Error:` mid-line; it adds to it rather than preventing it.

choices.text: Ending every message without punctuation
choices.why: Right. A message is a fragment that another layer may put in front of, never a closed sentence.

choices.text: Printing the error with `fmt.Printf` instead of `fmt.Println`
choices.why: The full stops are in the error's own text; any way of printing it shows them.

prompt: Of the 2,095 calls to `errors.New("…")` counted in Go 1.27.1's standard library, how many messages end with a full stop?
`fmt.Errorf("save notes: %w", reason)` with `reason` a `string`: what happens?

choices.text: The compiler refuses it
choices.why: To the compiler the format is just a string; `go run .` built and ran it.

choices.text: It panics when `fmt.Errorf` runs
choices.why: Nothing panicked; the message printed with the complaint inside it.

choices.text: It runs and prints `%!w(string=disk full)`; `go vet` reports it
choices.why: Right. `%w` needs an `error`, and vet checks the arguments against the format.

choices.text: `%w` turns the string into an error and wraps it
choices.why: No conversion happens; the documentation calls a non-error operand invalid.

prompt: `fmt.Errorf("start server: %___", err)` keeps `err` whole inside the error it returns.
hint: The verb that exists only in `fmt.Errorf`.

prompt: `validate("Ana", 30)` collected no problems and returned `errors.Join(errs...)` with an empty `errs`. What did it return?
hint: The first line of the output.

choices.text: An empty `*errors.joinError`, which is not nil
choices.why: That would be lesson 32's trap; `Join` avoids it and returns a real nil.

choices.text: `nil`
choices.why: Right. `Join` returns nil when every value, or no value, is nil, so `validate` needed no special case.

choices.text: An error whose message is the empty string
choices.why: It printed `<nil>`, not an empty line.

choices.text: It panicked, because `Join` needs at least one error
choices.why: It ran fine; the parameter is variadic and accepts zero values.

prompt: When does `fmt.Errorf` with two `%w` suit better than `errors.Join`?
hint: One line or several, your words or none.

choices.text: When there are more than two errors
choices.why: `Join` takes any number; the count is not what decides.

choices.text: When one of the errors may be nil
choices.why: That is a strength of `Join`, which discards nils; `fmt.Errorf` would print `%!w(<nil>)`.

choices.text: When the failures belong to one operation and should read as one sentence in your words
choices.why: Right. `save notes.txt: disk full (and closing it: …)` is one line; `Join` adds no words and puts each on its own line.

choices.text: When the errors must stay findable afterwards by callers, which `errors.Join` cannot offer
choices.why: Both keep every error whole; the documentation of `Join` says its errors may be inspected with `Is` and `As`.

prompt: Match each call to the type `%T` printed for its result.

A package's `Load` wraps `os.ReadFile`'s error with `%w`, and its users check for a missing file. Next release, `Load` reads from an embedded copy and never touches the disk. What happens to those users?

choices.text: Their code stops compiling until they remove the check
choices.why: Nothing in a signature changed, so everything compiles; that is why it is dangerous.

choices.text: Their check now matches every error `Load` returns
choices.why: The check looks for a file error, and no error from the new `Load` holds one.

choices.text: Their check compiles and runs, and its branch is dead from then on
choices.why: Right. Wrapping made the file error part of `Load`'s behaviour, and removing it broke users without a sign.

choices.text: Nothing, because wrapped errors are only text
choices.why: With `%w` the inner error is kept whole; that is exactly what they were relying on.

prompt: To add words to an error without letting callers reach the error underneath, `fmt.Errorf` uses the verb `%___`.
hint: The verb `Printf` uses for any value.

prompt: Which of these are good messages to put in front of a wrapped error? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lower case, no punctuation, what was being done.

choices.text: `"load user %d: %w"`
choices.why: Yes: a step, a value that identifies it, and the cause after the colon.

choices.text: `"Failed to load user: %w."`
choices.why: A capital, `Failed`, and a full stop: `~/wrap-style` showed what that does in the middle of a line.

choices.text: `"parse settings: %w"`
choices.why: Yes: it says what was being done and lets the cause finish the sentence.

choices.text: `"error: %w"`
choices.why: It says nothing the reader did not know: everything printed there is an error.

prompt: A function calls `os.Open` and then `json.Unmarshal`, and both can fail. A teammate wraps both with `%v` "to keep things simple". What does the caller lose compared with `%w`?
hint: The text is the same either way.

choices.text: The messages of the two errors
choices.why: `%v` prints the same text as `%w`; the messages are all there.

choices.text: Any way to tell from code which of the two failed, or why
choices.why: Right. `%v` keeps only text, so code can match nothing but strings, which section 02 advised against.

choices.text: The exit status of the program
choices.why: The status is whatever `main` passes to `os.Exit`; the verb has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Nothing at all; the two verbs are synonyms in `fmt.Errorf`
choices.why: They print alike and build different values: `*errors.errorString` against `*fmt.wrapError`.

prompt: A batch job processes 500 records and should report every record that fails, not just the first. Which shape fits?
hint: Section 04's form did the same with two fields.

choices.text: Return at the first failure, wrapped with `%w`
choices.why: That reports one record; the person fixes it and meets the next on the following run.

choices.text: One `fmt.Errorf` with a `%w` per record
choices.why: The format would need one verb per failure, and the number is not known when the code is written.

choices.text: Concatenate the messages into one string and pass the result to `errors.New`
choices.why: The text would be there, but every error underneath would be dropped, as with `%v`.

choices.text: Collect each record's error in a slice and return `errors.Join(errs...)`
choices.why: Right. Like `validate`, and it returns nil by itself when no record failed.
